# Weekly national flu and COVID-19 surveillance reports published

National influenza and COVID-19 report, monitoring coronavirus (COVID-19) activity, seasonal flu and other seasonal respiratory illnesses.

## Latest update

These updates are now published by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

## Previous updates

### Thursday 30 September 2021

The main points from this week’s national influenza and COVID-19 surveillance report are:

Surveillance indicators suggest that at a national level COVID-19 activity remained stable in most indicators in week 38 of 2021.

Case rates were highest in those aged 10 to 19, with a 7-day rate of 1084.2 per 100,000 population.

The lowest case rates were in those aged 80 and above, with a 7-day rate of 84.4 per 100,000 population.

Seven-day case rates per 100,000 population were highest in the East Midlands at 440.4.

Case rates per 100,000 were lowest in London with a 7-day rate of 201.9.

The number of acute respiratory infection incidents (suspected outbreaks) in England was 622 in week 38, compared to 544 in the previous week.

The hospital admission rate for week 38 was 5.26 per 100,000 population, in the previous week it was 6.46 per 100,000 population.

Hospital admission rates for COVID-19 were highest in the North East, with a rate of 9.73 per 100,000 population.

The highest hospital admission rates continue to be those aged 85 and above.

Meera Chand, COVID-19 Incident Director at Public Health England, said:

> Case rates remain high across the country, especially among young people.
>
> As we approach winter, everyone should keep following the simple steps to protect ourselves and others.
>
> Wear a face covering in enclosed spaces, avoid mixing with others if you feel unwell and get a PCR test straight away if you have any COVID-19 symptoms.
>
> The best way to protect yourself and others against COVID-19 is to get the vaccine – please make sure to get it if you are eligible.

### Thursday 23 September 2021

The main points from this week’s national influenza and COVID-19 surveillance report are:

Surveillance indicators suggest that at a national level COVID-19 activity remained stable or decreased in most indicators in week 37 of 2021.

Case rates were highest in those aged 10 to 19, with a 7-day rate of 756.2 per 100,000 population.

The lowest case rates were in those aged 80 and above, with a 7-day rate of 81.1 per 100,000 population.

Seven-day case rates per 100,000 population were highest in the East Midlands at 346.2.

Case rates per 100,000 were lowest in London with a 7-day rate of 182.3.

The number of acute respiratory infection incidents (suspected outbreaks) in England was 544 in week 37, compared to 541 in the previous week.

The hospital admission rate for week 37 was 6.36 per 100,000 population, in the previous week it was 7.37 per 100,000 population.

Hospital admission rates for COVID-19 were highest in the North East, with a rate of 10.34 per 100,000 population.

The highest hospital admission rates continue to be those aged 85 and above.

Dr Yvonne Doyle, Medical Director of Public Health England, said:

> We must remain vigilant as case rates remain high throughout the country. With winter approaching, it is likely that infections, hospitalisations and deaths will rise.
>
> The vaccines offer the best protection against COVID-19. One dose is now being offered to 12 to 15 year olds and a third dose to those over 50 and the clinically vulnerable.
>
> Please keep

This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 42 of 2026 between 12 October and 18 October 2026.

## Main points

The main messages of this report are:

* influenza activity remained stable and is circulating at baseline levels
* COVID-19 activity showed mixed trends and is circulating at low levels
* respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) showed mixed trends and is circulating at baseline levels

## Summary of all respiratory virus activity

### Influenza activity

Influenza activity remained stable and is circulating at baseline levels. Emergency department (ED) attendances for influenza-like illness (ILI) increased slightly at seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents in the community decreased compared with the previous week.

Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the third time this season. Data is for week 42 (up to 18 October 2026). Following issues with unavailable or incomplete influenza vaccination data at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42, several cohorts were not published in week 42. This has been corrected for this week’s report (week 43), and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting, but is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme.

Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 42 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (44.1% vs 49.3%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (19.9% vs 22.1%), 2-year-olds (26.0% vs 26.9%), and 3-year-olds (25.8% vs 26.8%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (26.0% vs 25.1%).
